title: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes
summary: Find hot code with a sampling profiler, read self time, total time, and callers, fix it and profile again, and time a program's stages with scoped timers.
intro: *Measuring Speed: Benchmarks, -O2, and Assembly* timed code you already suspected. In a real system you rarely know what to suspect: the backtest got slow, and it calls hundreds of functions. Guesses are usually wrong, and an afternoon spent speeding up a function that takes 2% of the time saves at most 2%. A **profiler** says where the time goes. This lesson shows how a sampling profiler works and how it differs from instrumentation, reads a real profile from this Mac's `sample` tool, fixes the hot spot it finds and profiles again, and adds scoped timers that count and time a program's stages by hand.

steps.title: Sampling against instrumentation
steps.body:
Your backtest takes three seconds, and it calls hundreds of functions. There are two ways to learn which of them the time goes to.

An **instrumenting** profiler adds code at the start and end of each function, or of each scope you mark, that counts the call and reads a clock. Its call counts and times are exact. But every call now pays for two clock reads, about 15 ns each on this Mac, so a function that takes 5 ns looks seven times slower than it is. Compilers can add such probes to every function (`-finstrument-functions`, and `-pg` for gprof), and the last part of this lesson writes them by hand.

A **sampling** profiler changes nothing in the program. Hundreds or thousands of times a second, a timer interrupts it, and the profiler records where it was: the program counter and the return addresses on the stack, its **call stack**, found by following the saved frame pointers from *Function Calls: Stack Frames, Registers, and the ABI*. Then it turns addresses into names with the symbol table, and into files and lines when you build with `-g`. A function that runs 30% of the time shows up in about 30% of the samples. That costs the program almost nothing and catches library and kernel code too, but it's statistics: no call counts, and a short function that runs rarely may never be caught.

| System | Sampling profilers |
| --- | --- |
| Linux | `perf record -g`, then `perf report` |
| macOS | `sample`, and Instruments' Time Profiler |
| Windows | Visual Studio's CPU Usage tool, Windows Performance Recorder |

Intel's VTune and AMD's uProf run on Linux and Windows. g++ at `-O2` leaves out frame pointers on x86-64, so build with `-fno-omit-frame-pointer` for `perf`, or record with `perf record --call-graph dwarf`. Apple's ARM64 code always keeps them. Instruments comes with Xcode: `xcrun xctrace record --template 'Time Profiler' --launch -- ./backtest` records a trace to open in it. This Mac has only the Command Line Tools, so it answers:

```text
xcrun: error: unable to find utility "xctrace", not a developer tool or in PATH
```

A sampler whose clock lines up with a loop's period keeps catching the same step of it, which is why `perf` users often sample at 99 Hz rather than 100. The example models both profilers on one simulated run.

example.title: A sampler and an instrumenter on one run
example.prompt: Simulate 10,000 ticks of a backtest on a clock in microseconds, count every call and its time as an instrumenter would, take a sample every 997 µs as a sampler would, and compare the two.
example.output:
101 samples over 101600 us
function     calls   time  samples  share
parse_tick   10000  19.7%       20  19.8%
send_order      40   1.6%        1   1.0%
signal       10000  49.2%       50  49.5%
update_book  10000  29.5%       30  29.7%
example.explanation:
`run` stands for one call that lasts `us` microseconds, and both profilers watch it. The instrumenter's part adds the call and its exact time. The sampler's `while` loop counts each sample time that falls before the call ends, then schedules the next sample. The run took 101,600 µs, so there were 101 samples, about one a millisecond, like `sample`'s default.

For the three steps that run on every tick, the sampled shares come within half a percent of the exact ones, from just 101 samples and at no cost to the program. `send_order` takes 1.6% of the time in 40 calls of 40 µs, and one sample caught it: a sampler can't tell 40 long calls from 4,000 short ones, while the instrumenter counted every call. Change `interval` to 1000 and nearly every sample lands at the same point of a 10 µs tick: `parse_tick` gets 98% of the samples, and `signal`, the slowest step, gets none.

steps.title: Reading a profile from sample
steps.body:
The nightly backtest takes three seconds for a day of 3 × 10^7 ticks, and the desk wants it under one. On every tick it calls `crossover_signal`, which compares a 100-tick mean with a 1000-tick mean, and `risk_ok`, which checks the price against a 500-tick mean. Both get their means from `window_mean(prices, end, window)`, which adds up the `window` prices before `end`. The whole program is the next part's example.

Profile the build you run, at `-O2`, with `-g` added for names and lines: `clang++ -std=c++17 -O2 -g -o backtest backtest.cpp`. While `./backtest slow 30000000` runs, `sample backtest 2 -file slow.txt` in a second terminal records its stack every millisecond for 2 seconds. The first profile named only `main`:

```text
1714 Thread_112108486   DispatchQueue_1: com.apple.main-thread  (serial)
  1714 start  (in dyld) + 7184
    1697 main  (in backtest) + 1076,1192,...  backtest.cpp:63
    17 main  (in backtest) + 1308  backtest.cpp:62
```

At `-O2`, clang inlined all three functions into `main`, so their samples carry `main`'s name and the line of the call. While you investigate, mark the suspects `[[gnu::noinline]]`, the attribute from *Function Calls: Stack Frames, Registers, and the ABI*. Then the profile names them (addresses trimmed, some lines left out):

```text
1716 Thread_112096285   DispatchQueue_1: com.apple.main-thread  (serial)
  1716 start  (in dyld) + 7184
    1023 main  (in backtest) + 484  backtest.cpp:63
    + 933 crossover_signal(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long)  (in backtest) + 52  backtest.cpp:20
    + ! 849 window_mean(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long, unsigned long)  (in backtest) + 84,76,...  backtest.cpp:13
    ...
    + 90 crossover_signal(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long)  (in backtest) + 32  backtest.cpp:20
    +   74 window_mean(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long, unsigned long)  (in backtest) + 84,144,...  backtest.cpp:13
    ...
    677 main  (in backtest) + 500  backtest.cpp:63
    + 676 risk_ok(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long)  (in backtest) + 36  backtest.cpp:25
    + ! 656 window_mean(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long, unsigned long)  (in backtest) + 84,76,...  backtest.cpp:13
    ...
Sort by top of stack, same collapsed (when >= 5):
        window_mean(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long, unsigned long)  (in backtest)        1699
        risk_ok(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long)  (in backtest)        7
        crossover_signal(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long)  (in backtest)        6
```

Every number counts samples, a millisecond each, and each function sits indented under its caller. The `+` and `!` only draw lines. `crossover_signal` appears twice, once for each of its two calls to `window_mean`, told apart by the return address's offset after its name: 933 samples for the 1000-tick mean and 90 for the 100-tick one, the ratio of the windows. A function's counts in the tree, added up over every place it appears, are its **total time**, with everything it called. The last list counts samples with the function on top of the stack, its **self time**: 1699 of 1716, 99%, inside `window_mean` itself. Its callers split them, 1023 through `crossover_signal` and 676 through `risk_ok`, so a fix inside `window_mean` speeds up both. `perf report` shows the same two numbers as Children and Self, and Instruments as Weight and Self Weight.

example.title: Self and total time from folded stacks
example.prompt: Write the Mac's profile as one line per stack, then add up each function's total time and self time and print them, largest total first.
example.output:
1716 samples
main              total 1704 (99.3%), self    4 ( 0.2%)
window_mean       total 1699 (99.0%), self 1699 (99.0%)
crossover_signal  total 1029 (60.0%), self    6 ( 0.3%)
risk_ok           total  683 (39.8%), self    7 ( 0.4%)
example.explanation:
Each entry in `folded` is one distinct stack from the profile, root first, with the thread and `start` left out, and the number of samples that caught it. That form is called **folded stacks**. The last frame was running, so it gets the self time. Every frame on the stack gets total time, and the `std::set` counts a function once per stack, so a recursive function isn't counted twice for one sample.

`main` has the largest total and almost no self time: it's on nearly every stack, waiting. `window_mean` has both, which makes it the one to fix. The 12 samples where `crossover_signal` or `risk_ok` has no `main` below it landed in the function's first or last few instructions, while the frame pointer still, or again, pointed at its caller's frame, so the stack walk skipped the caller. Real profiles always have a few of those.

Folded stacks are also what a **flame graph** draws. Each function on a stack is a box on top of its caller's box, as wide as its total samples, with siblings in alphabetical order, so left to right isn't time. The widest boxes are where the time goes, and the part of a box with nothing on top of it is self time. On Linux, Brendan Gregg's FlameGraph scripts draw one from `perf script` output, with `stackcollapse-perf.pl` and then `flamegraph.pl`, and Instruments and the speedscope viewer draw them too.

practice.title: Callers of a hot function
practice.prompt:
Read a profile in folded form and print which functions call a given one, with the samples each caller accounts for.

1. The first input line names the function. Every line after it is a stack, root first with frames joined by `;`, then a space and its sample count.
2. Split each stack into frames at `';'`. Wherever a frame is the function, add the count to `samples` and to its caller, the frame just before it, or to `(root)` when it's the first frame.
3. The starter prints the function's samples, then each caller with its count and share, most samples first.

The first test is a real profile from this Mac, of a fill monitor that looks for large fills.

Input:

```text
window_volume
main;is_spike;window_volume 734
main;is_busy;window_volume 117
main;is_busy 5
main 1
```

Expected output:

```text
window_volume: 851 samples
is_spike 734 (86.3%)
is_busy 117 (13.7%)
```

tests.stdin:
crossover_signal
main;crossover_signal;window_mean 1023
main;risk_ok;window_mean 676
main;risk_ok 1
crossover_signal 6
risk_ok 6
main 4

parse_price
main;on_packet;decode;parse_price 410
main;on_packet;decode 120
main;replay;decode;parse_price 95
main;on_packet;update_book;parse_price 95
main;on_packet;update_book 300

hints: Split the stack the way the example does: a `std::istringstream` over it and `std::getline(in, frame, ';')`.
Walk the frames by index, since the caller of `frames[i]` is `frames[i - 1]`, and use `"(root)"` when `i` is 0.
Add `count` to `samples` inside the same `if`, so a stack without the function adds nothing.

steps.title: Fixing the hot spot, then profiling again
steps.body:
Before fixing anything, see what a fix can buy. If a function takes a share p of the run and you make it s times faster, the whole run gets 1 / ((1 - p) + p / s) times faster. That's **Amdahl's law**, and even making the function free gives at most 1 / (1 - p). A function at 20% of the run can buy at most 1.25 times, however clever the fix, which is why you profile before you optimize:

```cpp
for (double p : {0.2, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99}) {
    std::cout << "a share of " << p << " made free: at most " << 1 / (1 - p) << " times faster\n";
}
```

At p = 0.99, fixing `window_mean` could make the backtest up to 100 times faster.

`window_mean` adds up 1600 prices per tick, 100, 1000, and 500 for the three windows, to learn something that changed by one price. A **running sum** keeps each window's total and, per tick, adds the newest price and subtracts the one leaving the window: two operations per window instead of hundreds. The prices are integer ticks, so the sums come out exactly the same. With `double` prices, a running sum would gather a rounding error with every step, one more reason for the integer ticks of *Numbers for Money: Floating Point and Integer Ticks*, later in this section.

The fix took the 3 × 10^7 ticks from 2.7 seconds to 0.08 on this Mac, too fast for `sample` to catch, so the second profile ran the fast version over 3 × 10^8 ticks (some lines left out):

```text
522 Thread_112099403   DispatchQueue_1: com.apple.main-thread  (serial)
  522 start  (in dyld) + 7184
    241 main  (in backtest) + 348  backtest.cpp:58
    146 main  (in backtest) + 884,888  backtest.cpp:70
    93 main  (in backtest) + 916,984,...  backtest.cpp:71
    38 main  (in backtest) + 1000,1028  backtest.cpp:73
    ...
```

`RollingMean::update` was inlined, so the lines tell the story. 46% of the samples were making the prices, on line 58, and the strategy's loop took the rest, spread over three lines with no hot spot left. In a real backtest the prices come from a file, so the next profile would look at the reading. Stop when the profile is flat or the program is fast enough. And after every change, check that the answer didn't change.

example.title: The backtest, slow and fixed
example.prompt: Run the backtest with window_mean adding up every window and with running sums, on the same 200,000 ticks, and check that both find the same flips and orders.
example.output:
slow: 330 flips, 308 orders
fast: 330 flips, 308 orders
example.explanation:
Both versions read the same prices, made once at the start from a seeded linear congruential generator, so they must agree, and they do: the signal changed sides 330 times, and 308 of those passed the risk check. That's the first check after any speed fix, since a faster program with a different answer is a bug.

A `RollingMean` must see every `end` in order from the first price, because its `sum` carries over. So the fast loop starts at `end = 1` and records only from 1000, the first tick with a full 1000-tick window, where the slow loop starts. The sandbox passes no arguments, so `version` is `both` and `n` is 200,000. On the Mac, `./backtest slow 30000000` runs one version over a whole day, which is how the profiles were taken. Built at `-O2` through the first line, the slow version took about 85 ms here and the fast one about 1.5 ms, rough times from the emulated sandbox.

practice.title: Fix the fill monitor's hot spot
practice.prompt:
Speed up a fill monitor's hot spot with running sums, and check that the fast loop counts what the slow one does.

The monitor counts spikes, fills over 8 times the average of the 1000 fills before them, and busy fills, when the last 200 fills traded over 200,000 shares. Here is the starter's slow part on the Mac over 4 × 10^7 fills, built with `-O2 -g` (addresses trimmed, some lines left out):

```text
857 Thread_112144262   DispatchQueue_1: com.apple.main-thread  (serial)
  857 start  (in dyld) + 7184
    734 main  (in spikes) + 236  spikes.cpp:47
    + 734 is_spike(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long)  (in spikes) + 40  spikes.cpp:17
    +   669 window_volume(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long, unsigned long)  (in spikes) + 88,80,...  spikes.cpp:10
    ...
    122 main  (in spikes) + 252  spikes.cpp:48
    + 117 is_busy(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long)  (in spikes) + 16  spikes.cpp:22
    + ! 93 window_volume(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long, unsigned long)  (in spikes) + 88,80  spikes.cpp:10
    ...
Sort by top of stack, same collapsed (when >= 5):
        window_volume(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long, unsigned long)  (in spikes)        851
        is_busy(std::vector<long long> const&, unsigned long)  (in spikes)        5
```

1. Finish `RollingSum::update`: add `qty[end - 1]` to `sum`, take away `qty[end - 1 - window]` once `end > window`, and return `sum`.
2. In `main`, make one pass over `end` from 1 to `n` with a `RollingSum` of 1000 and one of 200. Read the 1000-fill sum before you update it, since a spike compares a fill with the fills before it.
3. From `end` 1001 on, count the same spikes and busy fills as the slow loop, in `fast_spikes` and `fast_busy`.

The input is `n`.

Input:

```text
100000
```

Expected output:

```text
slow: 136 spikes, 5772 busy
fast: 136 spikes, 5772 busy
```

tests.output:
slow: 136 spikes, 5772 busy
fast: 136 spikes, 5772 busy

slow: 26 spikes, 1152 busy
fast: 26 spikes, 1152 busy

slow: 5 spikes, 388 busy
fast: 5 spikes, 388 busy

hints: `update` is the example's `RollingMean::update` without the division.
In the loop: `const int64_t prior = before.sum;` first, then `before.update(qty, end);` and `const int64_t last200 = recent.update(qty, end);`.
A spike is `qty[end - 1] * 1000 > 8 * prior`, and a busy fill is `last200 > 200000`, the slow functions' tests with your sums.

steps.title: Scoped timers and Google Benchmark

example.title: Probes in a quote handler
example.prompt: Time a quote handler, a block inside it, and the rare order it sends with scoped timers, then print each probe's call count.
example.output:
on_quote: 100000 calls
on_quote/book: 100000 calls
send_order: 480 calls
orders sent 480
example.explanation:
Each `static Probe&` line runs `probes["..."]` once, on that function's first call, which creates the probe and keeps a reference to it. A `std::map` never moves its elements, so the reference stays good as other probes are added. The inner block has a probe of its own, and its closing brace destroys that `ScopedTimer`, so `on_quote/book` times the book update alone.

The counts are exact, which no sampler gives: 100,000 quotes, and an order for each of the 480 bids that were a multiple of 250. Times change every run, so the line that prints them is commented out. Uncommented and built at `-O2`, `on_quote/book` reported about 21 ns per call, here and on the Mac, for a single store: nearly all of it is the two clock reads. `on_quote` reported about 70 ns, its own two reads plus the inner probe's. A probe that fine measures the probe, so real code puts them around whole stages.

practice.title: Probes in a risk check
practice.prompt:
Time a pre-trade risk check with scoped timers, and see from the counts which checks really run.

1. Finish `~ScopedTimer`: add the nanoseconds since `start_` to `probe_.ns`, and one to `probe_.calls`.
2. Time `size_ok`, `price_ok`, and `check_order` with a probe named after each, looked up once through a `static Probe&`.
3. The starter reads the last trade price, then one order per line, `<qty> <price>`, and prints each probe's count in name order, then the totals. A probe that never ran was never created, so it isn't printed.

Input:

```text
19275
100 19280
5000 19275
200 19400
50 19250
0 19275
```

Expected output:

```text
check_order: 5 calls
price_ok: 3 calls
size_ok: 5 calls
2 accepted, 3 rejected
```

tests.output:
check_order: 5 calls
price_ok: 3 calls
size_ok: 5 calls
2 accepted, 3 rejected

check_order: 2 calls
size_ok: 2 calls
0 accepted, 2 rejected

check_order: 3 calls
price_ok: 3 calls
size_ok: 3 calls
3 accepted, 0 rejected

hints: The destructor is the example's: `const auto elapsed = std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - start_;`, then add `std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(elapsed).count()`.
Start each function with `static Probe& probe = probes["size_ok"];` and `ScopedTimer timer(probe);`, with that function's name.
`price_ok` runs fewer times than `size_ok` because `&&` skips it when `size_ok` is false.

recap:
- A sampling profiler interrupts the program hundreds or thousands of times a second and records its call stack. It costs almost nothing, but it gives shares, not counts, and it can miss short, rare calls.
- An instrumenting profiler counts and times every call exactly, at the cost of the probes themselves.
- Profile the `-O2` build with `-g`: `perf record -g` and `perf report` on Linux, `sample` or Instruments' Time Profiler on a Mac, Visual Studio's profiler on Windows. `perf` on x86-64 needs `-fno-omit-frame-pointer` or `--call-graph dwarf`.
- Inlined functions show up as their caller's lines. Mark the suspects `[[gnu::noinline]]` while you investigate.
- Self time counts the samples with a function on top of the stack, and total time includes everything it called. Fix the function with the self time, and look at its callers.
- Folded stacks list each stack once with its count, and a flame graph draws them: a box's width is its total time, and the part with nothing on top is self time.
- Amdahl's law: making a share p of the run free speeds it up at most 1 / (1 - p) times.
- After a fix, check that the answer is unchanged, then profile again. Stop when the profile is flat or the program is fast enough.
- A scoped timer is RAII around two `steady_clock` reads. Look its probe up once and time whole stages. Google Benchmark compares small functions.
